title: Open umbilical and incisional hernia repair with mesh
subtitle: Sublay (retromuscular) and preperitoneal mesh

sources.org: European Hernia Society and Americas Hernia Society
sources.title: Guidelines on the treatment of primary umbilical and epigastric hernias
Classification of primary and incisional abdominal wall hernias
Guidelines on the closure of abdominal wall incisions

indications: Symptomatic umbilical, paraumbilical, epigastric or incisional hernia.
Incarceration, obstruction or strangulation as an emergency, where the mesh plan depends on contamination.
Hernias with thinning or ulcerated overlying skin.
Asymptomatic small hernias may be observed after discussion; the decision is shared rather than default.
contraindications: Active infection or contamination in the field, for permanent synthetic mesh.

Modifiable risk factors not yet addressed for an elective repair: active smoking, poorly controlled diabetes and obesity increase wound complications and recurrence, and many units optimise these before elective surgery.
Uncontrolled ascites, which causes wound leak and recurrence until it is managed.
Loss of domain or very wide defects need specialist planning, not an unplanned repair.
preparation: Examine standing and lying, and define the defect clinically. Cross-sectional imaging helps for incisional, recurrent, multiple or large hernias and in obesity.
Optimise smoking, glycaemic control and weight where time allows.
Review the previous operation notes for an incisional hernia: previous mesh, stomas and bowel surgery change the plan.

Consent must include recurrence, seroma, haematoma, wound infection and skin necrosis, mesh infection that may need mesh removal, chronic pain, injury to bowel with possible resection, loss or altered appearance of the umbilicus, and the possibility of a different repair than planned.
Mark the hernia with the patient standing.
positioning: Supine, arms out, with the abdomen exposed from the costal margins to the pubis for an incisional hernia.
Urinary catheter for long incisional repairs or those extending to the pubis.
equipment: Major general set with long instruments and deep retractors.
Synthetic mesh suitable for the extraperitoneal plane, in sizes larger than the expected need.
Slowly absorbable monofilament for posterior and anterior closure.
Closed suction drains if the unit uses them.
anatomy: The rectus sheath is formed by the aponeuroses of the three lateral muscles; above the arcuate line it has anterior and posterior layers, below it only an anterior layer, with the rectus resting on transversalis fascia and peritoneum.
The linea alba is the midline fusion of the sheaths; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral edge of the rectus.
The segmental intercostal nerves and vessels run between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis and enter the rectus through its posterior aspect near the linea semilunaris.
The umbilicus is a natural weak point in the linea alba; paraumbilical hernias emerge through the linea alba just above or below it.
The European Hernia Society classifies ventral hernias by location (midline or lateral zones) and width.
criticalSafety: Expect bowel adherent to the sac and scar, and dissect it under direct vision.
Preserve the lateral neurovascular bundles: they are the lateral limit of the retromuscular plane.
Close the posterior layer completely so the mesh does not contact bowel.
Do not place permanent synthetic mesh in a contaminated field without a deliberate senior decision.
Close the anterior fascia without tension; if it will not close, stop and seek help.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel and omentum adherent to the sac
Bladder in a low incisional hernia
commonErrors: Missing additional defects along an incisional scar.
Dissection extended beyond the linea semilunaris.
Unrepaired holes in the posterior layer.
Closing fascia under tension, causing early recurrence and pain.
complications: Surgical site infection and skin necrosis, more likely with smoking, diabetes and obesity.
Mesh infection, sometimes requiring mesh removal.
Chronic pain and abdominal wall bulging from denervation.
Venous thromboembolism after major incisional repair.
postop: Day case for small primary hernias; admission for larger incisional repairs.
Early mobilisation, thromboprophylaxis according to risk, and multimodal analgesia.
Remove drains when output has fallen to the threshold the unit uses, and record the decision.
Review promptly for wound redness, discharge, fever or new abdominal pain and distension.
Advise a gradual return to activity guided by comfort; an abdominal binder may help comfort but is not proven to reduce recurrence.

steps.emphasis: Mark the hernia standing and record whether the umbilicus may be excised.
Open the sac to divide adhesions under vision in incisional hernias; a small umbilical sac may simply be reduced.
A suction drain in the retromuscular or subcutaneous space is a unit decision; bring it out through separate clean skin away from the mesh.
Check the perforating vessels in the retromuscular plane before closing over the mesh: a haematoma here becomes a mesh infection.
Close the anterior sheath over the mesh with a small-bite technique and a suture length to wound length ratio of at least four to one, without tension.
Send excised omentum or bowel; the sac and skin are sent if they look abnormal.
Reattach the umbilical stalk to the fascia to restore the umbilicus, and close dead space without strangulating fat.

step.vhr.incision.title: Incision and exposure of the hernia
step.vhr.incision.why: The incision has to reach healthy fascia in every direction around the defect and must not devascularise the skin. For an umbilical hernia it also decides whether the patient keeps a normal-looking umbilicus.
how: Umbilical or paraumbilical: a curved infraumbilical or supraumbilical incision at the edge of the umbilicus, sized to the defect.
Incisional: excise the old scar through a midline incision, removing thin or ulcerated skin, but keep enough skin for closure without tension.
Dissect down to the sac and around it to the fascial edge, keeping the subcutaneous fat attached to the skin to preserve its blood supply.
Avoid raising wide skin flaps off the anterior sheath; they cause seroma and wound necrosis.
structuresAtRisk: Umbilical skin and its blood supply
Bowel stuck to the underside of a thin sac
pitfalls: Cutting straight down into a sac that lies just under thin skin and entering adherent bowel.
Wide subcutaneous flaps that become a seroma cavity.
Detaching the umbilical stalk from the skin without planning to reattach it.

step.vhr.defect-assess.title: Measuring the defect and choosing the repair
step.vhr.defect-assess.why: The repair is chosen after the fascia is defined, not from the clinic note. Incisional hernias often have several defects along the scar, and the width of the defect, not its length, decides whether closure without tension is possible.
how: Define the fascial edges all round, then palpate and inspect the whole length of the previous incision for further defects.
Measure the width and length of the defect, and classify it using the EHS system (location and width) for the record.

For a primary umbilical or epigastric hernia, the EHS and AHS guideline suggests mesh repair for most defects, with suture repair considered for very small defects; use the guideline thresholds your unit has adopted.

For an incisional hernia, plan a retromuscular (sublay) mesh with wide overlap. If the fascia cannot be closed over the mesh without tension, stop and get senior help: a component separation or staged approach may be needed.
Record the measurements, the number of defects and the chosen repair in the note.
structuresAtRisk: Fascia, which tears if closure is forced
Bowel adherent to the margins of the defect
pitfalls: Repairing one defect and missing a second along the same scar.
Committing to primary suture of a wide defect that will only close under tension.
Measuring the skin opening rather than the fascial defect.

step.vhr.retrorectus.title: Developing the retromuscular plane
step.vhr.retrorectus.why: The retromuscular space between the rectus muscle and the posterior sheath is well vascularised and separated from the bowel, so a mesh there is protected and integrates well. Dissection that goes beyond the linea semilunaris divides the nerves that supply the rectus and causes muscle denervation and bulging.
how: Incise the posterior rectus sheath about half to one centimetre from its medial edge, on each side, so a strong medial edge remains for closure.
Lift the rectus muscle off the posterior sheath with blunt dissection, controlling perforating vessels as they are met.
Stop laterally before the linea semilunaris, where the intercostal neurovascular bundles enter the posterior aspect of the rectus; they mark the lateral limit.
Below the arcuate line, where there is no posterior sheath, continue in the preperitoneal plane down to the space of Retzius if the defect is low.
Extend the plane far enough above and below the defect to allow the overlap the mesh needs.
structuresAtRisk: Intercostal neurovascular bundles at the lateral edge of the posterior sheath
Inferior epigastric vessels on the posterior surface of the rectus
Bowel beneath a thin posterior sheath
pitfalls: Dividing the neurovascular bundles at the lateral edge of the plane, denervating the rectus muscle.
Buttonholing the posterior sheath and then placing the mesh against bowel.
Incising the posterior sheath at its very edge, leaving nothing to suture.

step.vhr.posterior-closure.title: Closing the posterior layer
step.vhr.posterior-closure.why: The posterior sheath and peritoneum separate the mesh from the bowel. A gap in this layer exposes mesh to bowel, risking adhesions, erosion and fistula.
how: Close the posterior sheath and peritoneum in the midline with a continuous slowly absorbable suture, including any opened sac edges.
Repair every buttonhole made during the dissection.
If the posterior layer will not meet without tension, do not force it: use the omentum or the sac to bridge a small gap, and seek senior help for anything larger.
Protect the bowel with a malleable retractor or the assistant's hand while suturing.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel immediately beneath the posterior layer
pitfalls: Leaving small holes in the posterior layer that later let bowel touch the mesh.
Catching bowel in the posterior sheath suture.

step.vhr.mesh-sublay.title: Placing the mesh in the sublay position
step.vhr.mesh-sublay.why: In sublay the mesh is held in place by intra-abdominal pressure against the rectus muscles, and the overlap beyond the defect, not the number of sutures, prevents recurrence.
how: Size the mesh to overlap the defect generously in every direction; incisional repairs need wider overlap than primary umbilical repairs.
Lay the mesh flat on the closed posterior layer, extending into the dissected space, with no folds.
Fixation in the retromuscular plane is often limited or omitted when the overlap is wide; if used, avoid transfascial sutures near the lateral neurovascular bundles.
For a primary umbilical or paraumbilical hernia, a flat mesh in the preperitoneal or retromuscular plane through the same incision follows the same principles on a smaller scale.
Confirm the mesh lies flat once more before closing the anterior sheath over it.
structuresAtRisk: Intercostal nerves with lateral transfascial sutures
Bowel if the posterior layer is breached
pitfalls: A mesh cut small to fit a limited dissection.
Mesh folded at the edges of the space.
Leaving mesh in contact with the subcutaneous fat because the anterior sheath was not closed.
